title: Internal Revenue Code of 1954: Corporate Tax Loopholes Codified
description: President Eisenhower signs the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 into law on August 16, following final Congressional passage on July 29. This represents the first complete revision of the U.S. tax code since 1876, 'renumbering every section' and 'making over 3,000 technical changes in the law.' While maintaining the top corporate tax rate at 52% through March 1955 (extended through 1963), the code creates numerous corporate-friendly provisions including enhanced depreciation deductions with additional schedules, better tax treatment for research and development costs, a new simplified system for small corporations, and reduced 'penalty tax on accumulated earnings when necessary for legitimate business purposes.' The code extends net operating loss carry-backs and creates a 4% dividend tax credit for individual shareholders. President Eisenhower praised the bill in his January 7, 1954 State of the Union address, recommending 25 specific provisions including 'special relief' measures. The code's '3,000 technical changes' embed countless deductions, credits, and exceptions that reduce effective corporate tax rates well below the 52% statutory rate. Many features from the 1954 code survive until the Tax Reform Act of 1986 and some continue today.

sources.title: Statement by the President Upon Signing Bill Revising the Internal Revenue Code

significance: The 3,000 technical changes represent triumph of corporate tax lobbying—creating complex code that appears to maintain high rates (52%) while embedding numerous loopholes, deductions, and special provisions that dramatically reduce effective tax burden. The code's complexity makes it difficult for citizens to understand actual corporate tax burden versus statutory rates. The 30-year survival of this code (until 1986) demonstrates success of corporate influence in tax policy. This establishes pattern of using 'technical complexity' to obscure corporate tax benefits, a strategy that continues in every subsequent tax code revision.
